questions.question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

My mother said / that the thief / Ramesh will learnt / his lesson soon.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '1' i.e. Ramesh will learnt .

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given sentence contains an error in the phrase **"Ramesh will learnt"**.
 
• The word **"learnt"** is the past tense or past participle form of the verb** "learn" **and cannot follow **"will"** because **"will"** is followed by the base form of the verb.
 
• The correct form is **"Ramesh will learn"**.

Correct sentence: *My mother said that the thief Ramesh will learn his lesson soon*.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Usage of "will":** In future tense sentences, the auxiliary verb **"will"** is always followed by the base form of the main verb.
 
• **Example:** She **will go** to the market tomorrow (correct).
 
• **Incorrect:** She **will went** to the market tomorrow (incorrect).

questions.question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.

After the match, / the stadium was the messiest / it's ever been.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **No error**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The sentence is grammatically correct.
 
• The correctness lies in the use of **"it's ever been."** The contraction **"it's"** stands for **"it is"** or **"it has."** In this context, "it has" aligns properly with the intended meaning.
 
• The correct phrase should be **"it has ever been"** to match the past perfect context of the sentence.
 
• The sentence describes the state of the stadium after the match, comparing it to how messy it has been in the past.

Correct sentence: *After the match, the stadium was the messiest it has ever been.*

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate adjective to fill in the blank.

According to the chairman, his proposal was _________ than Mr. Jackson's.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '1' i.e. worse .

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence **compares **the chairman's proposal to Mr. Jackson's proposal. This is a comparative sentence.
 
• In **comparative **sentences, the correct **adjective **form to use is the **comparative degree** (e.g., worse, better, etc.) rather than the base form (e.g., bad) or the superlative degree (e.g., worst).
 
• The adjective** "worse"** is the **comparative degree** of "bad," which fits the context of the sentence.

Correct sentence: *According to the chairman, his proposal was **worse** than Mr. Jackson's.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Comparative Degree:**

 
 
• **Usage:** Used to compare two things.
 
• **Example:** This book is better than that one.
 
 
 
• **Superlative Degree:**
 
 
• **Usage:** Used to compare more than two things and indicate the highest degree.
 
• **Example:** This is the best book of all.

questions.question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error in phrasal verb.

Gita got onto / the book / she was reading / this morning.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '3' i.e. Gita got onto .

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The phrasal verb **"got onto"** is incorrect in this context.
 
• It is typically used to mean 'to board' (e.g., a bus or train) or 'to start talking about a subject.' However, it does not fit when referring to reading a book.
 
• The correct phrasing should be **"Gita got into the book"**, which means she became deeply engaged or interested in reading the book.
 
• Using the wrong phrasal verb leads to a misinterpretation or an awkward construction in the sentence.

Correct sentence: *Gita got into the book she was reading this morning*.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Commonly used phrasal verbs:**

 
 
• **Get into:** To become interested or engaged in something (e.g., a hobby, a book).
 
• **Get on:** To board a vehicle like a bus or train.
 
• **Get over:** To recover from an illness or emotional setback.
 
• **Get onto:** To start discussing a topic or board a vehicle.
 
 
 
• Using the correct phrasal verb is crucial for conveying the intended meaning and avoiding miscommunication.

questions.question:
In the following sentence the underlined part contains an error. Alternatives to the underlined part are given as options. Select the correct alternative.

Wolffia is the __tiny__ plant in the world.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '2' i.e. tiniest .

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence states that **Wolffia** is the smallest plant in the world, which requires the use of the **superlative degree** of the adjective "tiny."
 
• The use of** 'the'** before the underlined part of the sentence hints at the fact that a superlative degree must be used in this context.
 
• The superlative form of "tiny" is "**tiniest**," which is used to express that something is the smallest or most extreme in its category.

Correct sentence: *Wolffia is the tiniest plant in the world*.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Degrees of Comparison:**

 
 
• **Positive Degree:** Used when no comparison is made (e.g., "This plant is tiny.").
 
• **Comparative Degree:** Used to compare two things (e.g., "This plant is tinier than that one.").
 
• **Superlative Degree:** Used to compare one thing with a group or category, indicating the extreme degree (e.g., "This is the tiniest plant.").
 
 
 
• **Superlative Forms:** Superlative adjectives often end in "**-est**" for short adjectives like "tiny," or use "**most**" for longer adjectives (e.g., "most beautiful").
